entries.title: Federal judge told 'things are no longer quiet' as Midway Blitz lawsuit faces critical November ruling
entries.summary: <p>The judge who once challenged<b> </b>Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino<b> </b>and tried to limit the feds’ use of force<b> </b>during Operation Midway Blitz<b> </b>is now expected to decide in mid-November whether she’ll allow <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/12/illinois-chicago-sue-trump-administration-over-organized-bombardment-under-noem-bovino" target="_blank" >Illinois and Chicago’s<b> </b>lawsuit</a> over the deportation campaign<b> </b>to move forward.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis<b> </b>said she will rule Nov. 17 on Homeland Security’s<b> </b>bid to have the lawsuit tossed out. She set the ruling date after listening to three-and-a-half hours<b> </b>of arguments Wednesday in the same courtroom where she once <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/24/federal-judge-orders-border-patrol-commander-greg-bovino-into-her-courtroom" target="_blank" >ordered Bovino to appear</a>. </p><p>The arguments came with Chicago on the cusp of marking the one-year anniversary of Midway Blitz. It began Sept. 8, 2025,<b> </b>and led to eight weeks of chaos, tear gas and fear. The feds say the campaign<b> </b>ended<b> </b>late in 2025, but Illinois’ lawyers clearly aren’t convinced.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/12/illinois-chicago-sue-trump-administration-over-organized-bombardment-under-noem-bovino" >Trump administration hit with federal lawsuit over ‘occupation of Illinois and Chicago’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>In fact, attorneys recently<b> </b>accused the feds of resuming<b> </b>their use of chemical munitions, warrantless arrests and enforcement activity near sensitive locations like courthouses. Chicago’s immigration court<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/24/chaotic-crowded-chicago-immigration-mega-court-hearings-are-fueling-record-deportation-orders" target="_blank" >led the country<b> </b>in hearings</a><b> </b>in June.</p><p>“Things are no longer quiet,” Illinois attorney Vikas<b> </b>Didwania<b> </b>told Ellis in a court filing last week.</p><p>The lawsuit alleges the Trump administration “unleashed an organized bombardment on the State of Illinois and the City of Chicago”<b> </b>designed to “coerce”<b> </b>them<b> </b>into abandoning sanctuary policies, which mean local authorities won’t help track down immigrants without legal status.</p><p>Among other things, it asks Ellis to block similar future attempts at immigration enforcement by Homeland Security and U.S. Customs and Border Protection.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" >Judge blasts Trump’s Chicago border ‘Blitz,’ extends curbs on use of force that ‘shocks the conscience’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Ellis, appointed to the bench by then-President Barack Obama in 2013, took over the case after handling similar litigation last fall. She’d <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >entered a preliminary injunction</a><b> </b>Nov. 6<b> </b>that limited the feds’ use of force<b> </b>during the campaign, reading<b> </b>Carl Sandburg’s<b> </b>“Chicago”<b> </b>poem<b> </b>as she ruled.</p><p>The 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals blocked<b> </b>and later vacated her order.</p><p>Wednesday’s hearing in the new case largely turned on technical legal arguments, including whether Illinois and Chicago have the right to sue. But Ellis and the lawyers explored the differences between the 2025 campaign and the aggressive, albeit quieter, immigration enforcement that’s now ongoing.</p><p>The judge also reflected on an effort to enforce one of her orders last fall.</p><p>Ellis brought it up while asking the lawyers to identify the line between legitimate immigration enforcement and the kind of coercion alleged by Illinois and Chicago. She wanted to know, “at what point do I … step out of my lane?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Gregory Bovino walks out of the Dirksen Federal Courthouse after testifying during a hearing about immigration enforcement in Chicago, Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. | Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Before she handed down her injunction last fall, Ellis had entered a similar temporary restraining order. Then, in late October, she ordered Bovino<b> </b>to appear in her courtroom<b> </b>to discuss whether that order was being followed. The former Border Patrol official, who became the public face of Midway Blitz, has since retired.</p><p>“I had issued a valid order saying, ‘this is what can be used, this is the amount of force that is appropriate in this particular setting,’” Ellis said Wednesday, “and it was certainly my impression that that order was not being followed, right?”</p><p>The judge then tried to force Bovino to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/28/border-patrol-gregory-bovino-federal-court" target="_blank" >return to her courtroom</a> regularly, over the course of a week. She explained Wednesday that she’d wanted to “look backwards”<b> </b>with him on events that had already transpired. Had she asked him to tell her what he was doing the next day, she said, that would have amounted to her improperly “managing”<b> </b>the executive branch.</p><p>But there wound up being “a difference of opinion on whether that violated the separation of powers”<b> </b>between the courts and the executive branch, she said.</p><p>The federal appeals court<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/31/bovinos-daily-meetings-with-judge-would-infringe-on-separation-of-powers-appeals-court-says" target="_blank" >ruled that it did</a>.</p><p>“I think that it is very illustrative of how tricky that can be,” Ellis told the lawyers Wednesday.</p><p>Justice Department<b> </b>attorney Brantley<b> </b>Mayers<b> </b>argued that Illinois and Chicago want to have it both ways: They don’t want to support the federal government’s immigration efforts, and they don’t want the feds to be allowed to deploy more resources to do it on its own.</p><p>But Ellis told him, “I don’t think that’s what they’re arguing, at all.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/05/crucial-hearing-over-feds-use-of-force-could-reveal-incredible-bovino-testimony-wednesday" >‘It’s a disgrace': Chicagoans describe jarring encounters with feds as judge prepares to rule on ‘blitz’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“What they are complaining about, at this point, is that there were a number of warrantless arrests,” Ellis said. “That people were being stopped on the street. That people were being stopped dropping off their kids to school. That people were being stopped going to church. Going to the grocery store. That people living in an apartment complex had agents in the middle of the night rappelling down the side of their building and coming in.</p><p>“That that sort of behavior, combined with the treatment of people who were protesting the increased enforcement … that that crossed the line from enforcement to coercion.”</p><p>Lee Reeves, Mayers’ co-counsel, told the judge the lawsuit was brought by the wrong claimants making the wrong claims. He said individuals who claim to have been harmed during the campaign should be pursuing lawsuits or criminal charges, instead.</p><p>Several individuals have done exactly that. And many have called for federal agents to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/jon-seidel?p=00000198-1631-d49b-af99-df3def400000.2" target="_blank" >face criminal charges</a> for alleged wrongdoing during Midway Blitz.</p><p>Meanwhile, Illinois attorney Paul<b> </b>Berks invited the feds to make another claim: That the lawsuit is “moot.” In other words, there’s no reason to worry about Midway Blitz happening again.</p><p>Reeves and<b> </b>Mayers<b> </b>did not take him up on the offer.</p><p>“We would love to see the evidence that it’s not going to happen again,” Berks said.</p>

entries.title: Even on night bats bash Jacob Misiorowski, eyes on bullpen as Jacob Webb takes liner off arm in Cubs loss
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> can’t shake <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/02/cubs-bullpen-relief-pitchers-stats-daniel-palencia-jacob-webb-trent-thornton-justin-steele-javier-assad-edward-cabrera-pedro-ramirez" >their bullpen blues</a>.</p><p>Even on a night the Cubs’ bats did the unthinkable and scorched Cy Young favorite <b>Jacob Misiorowski</b> for five runs – the Brewers’ fireballing ace hadn’t given up more than three earned runs in a start this season – the story was what the team’s pitching staff couldn’t do in a 9-5 loss: keep their division-leading rivals at bay.</p><p>Lefty starter <b>David Peterson</b> was the main culprit, coughing up a 5-3 lead and getting tagged for six runs without getting out of the fourth inning.</p><p>But a relief corps that’s struggled lately grabbed negative headlines again, with righty closer <b>Jacob Webb</b> knocked out of the game in the top of the ninth inning after taking a line-drive comebacker off his right forearm.</p><p>Manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> updated after the game that X-rays were negative.</p><p>Though he’s been the team’s top reliever this season, Webb – who was charged with a couple runs after departing Wednesday – has contributed the loudest moments of a sour stretch for the bullpen, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/26/cubs-walk-off-loss-diamondbacks-clay-holmes-kevin-gausman-daniel-palencia-jacob-webb-bullpen" >surrendering walk-off homers in consecutive appearances</a> on the Cubs’ most recent road trip.</p><p>But he hasn’t been alone, with righty <b>Trent Thornton</b> tagged for six runs in two outings against the Reds last weekend and <b>Daniel Palencia</b> balking a runner home and allowing a game-flipping homer in Tuesday’s loss.</p><p>Palencia gave up a run Wednesday, too, and he’s got a 14.54 ERA in five outings since returning from the IL.</p><p>“We need Daniel. The results have not been good,” Counsell said after the game. “The best thing we can do is get him out there as much as we can.</p><p>“We need our bullpen guys to get outs, and Daniel’s one of the key guys we need to get going. We’re going to keep putting him out there.”</p><p>There will be more to come on Webb’s status, but any missed time would be a big problem for the Cubs as they look to right their relief ship in time to count on their bullpen arms in the postseason.</p><p>“Hopefully he can get back soon,” third baseman <b>Alex Bregman</b> said.</p><p><b>Making a mess of ‘The Miz’</b></p><p>He’s “The Miz” and nobody beats him?</p><p>Most days. But not Wednesday.</p><p>The Cubs struck early, with Bregman smacking a two-run, first-inning homer. Outfielder <b>Tyrone Taylor</b>’s RBI single and a Bregman two-out, two-run base hit added three runs in the second.</p><p>Though the Cubs started the day with baseball’s highest scoring offense, they’d faced Misiorowski twice previously this summer and managed only one run against him in 12 innings.</p><p>This time, they chased him from the game after four innings, matching his shortest start of the campaign.</p><p>“It was a pass-the-line night against Misiorowski,” Counsell said, “and that’s a pretty darn good job.”</p><p>They weren’t as successful against the Brewers’ bullpen, though, mustering only two hits after the second inning, and the Cubs fell to nine games back in the NL Central standings.</p>

entries.title: Police warn of strong-arm robberies and thefts on Northwest Side
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are alerting the public to recent strong-arm robberies and thefts from vehicles in the Portage Park and Irving Park neighborhoods.</p><p>Police believe the alleged thieves, which were reported from late July through Wednesday morning.<br>targeted people at banks and gas stations, typically during daytime hours, according to an alert.</p><p>In some instances, police said the assailants have entered occupied vehicles and taken items. During some thefts, the alleged perpetrators wait until the car is empty, steal money or other items, and flee to a car waiting nearby. </p><p>Police said during these robberies, the alleged offenders have not spoken to the victims or displayed weapons.</p><p>The thefts reported so far include the following locations: <br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-dc9f1f32-a73f-11f1-8dbf-9bb0082d645b"><li>6400 block of West Irving Park Road on July 23 at 1:05 p.m. </li><li>3200 block of West Irving Park Road on July 27 at 12:23 p.m. </li><li>4400 block of North Central Avenue on Aug. 5 at 12:43 p.m. </li><li>3200 block of West Irving Park Road on Aug. 11 at 10:48 a.m. </li><li>5200 block of North Cicero Avenue on Aug. 16 at 5:05 p.m. </li><li>3900 block of North Kilpatrick Avenue on Aug. 18 at 10:57 a.m. </li><li>4600 block of West Irving Park Road on Aug. 31 at 1:30 p.m. </li><li>5600 block of West Montrose Avenue on Sept. 2 at 11:43 a.m. </li></ul><p>Police described the suspects as two men dressed in black and wearing black face masks.</p><p>The vehicles being used by the alleged assailants include a black Nissan Rogue, a black Lincoln SUV, and a black Porsche Macan, police said.</p><p>Residents are encouraged to be aware of their surroundings and report any suspicious activity immediately, police said.</p><p>Anyone with information is encouraged to contact Area 5 detectives at 312-746-7394 or submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com and provide reference number P26-5-014.</p>

entries.title: Hersh’s Fridge dedicated in Skokie in memory of Hersh Goldberg-Polin
entries.summary: <p>A kosher community fridge honoring Hersh Goldberg-Polin, a 23-year-old with Chicago ties who was taken hostage and later killed by Hamas, was dedicated Wednesday in Skokie.</p><p>Hersh’s Fridge, which organizers describe as the country’s first kosher community fridge, is open 24 hours a day and offers prepared meals, produce, groceries and dry goods to anyone who needs them.</p><p>The project grew from the work of Solu, an Orthodox Jewish bridge-building initiative, executive director Rabbi Hody Nemes said.</p><p>Nemes said the community drew inspiration from community fridges in Chicago and Evanston.</p><p>Solu volunteers had also stocked non-kosher fridges and had wondered about creating a kosher fridge serving the Jewish community and its neighbors, he said.</p><p>For several years, the idea seemed like a “pipe dream,” Nemes said.</p><p>Goldberg-Polin was taken hostage in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack in Israel. A group met Sept. 1, 2024 — the day after learning Goldberg-Polin’s body had been found in a tunnel in Gaza — to consider whether the kosher fridge idea was feasible.</p><p>When the group watched a livestream of Goldberg-Polin’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/israel-hamas-war/2024/09/22/american-hostage-hersh-goldberg-polin-israel-hamas-gaza-oct7-memorial-skokie" target="_blank" >funeral</a>, they heard his parents say, “May his memory be a revolution,” Nemes said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> entries.title: Torrence Avenue Bridge reopens after being stuck due to heat-related issue
entries.summary: <p>Commuters faced headaches in multiple directions Wednesday as the Torrence Avenue Bridge got stuck in the raised position late Wednesday afternoon, just hours after the DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge reopened following a similar occurrence.</p><p>The bridge — located over the Calumet River — was stuck for more than an hour, starting at 4:30 p.m., according to Erica Schroeder, director of public affairs for the Chicago Department of Transportation.</p><p>Schroeder confirmed the issue with the Torrence Avenue bridge this afternoon was heat-related.</p><p>"Thermal expansion caused by the high temperatures affected the bridge’s operation," Schroeder explained.</p><p>CDOT crews responded to the scene and returned the bridge to its normal operating position, Schroeder said. The bridge reopened to traffic shortly after 5:30 p.m., she said.</p><p>The city’s Office of Emergency Management and Communications <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/ChicagoOEMC/status/2095290854676038104?s=20" target="_blank" ><u>confirmed</u></a> via social media at 6:20 p.m. that the Torrence Avenue Bridge had been “stuck in the up position” and said hot weather caused the issue. The office urged drivers to use alternate routes.</p><p>The DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge had become <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/02/lake-shore-drive-bridge-river" target="_blank" ><u>stuck open</u></a> during a routine lift around 10 a.m., leaving it off-limits to drivers for more than four hours before returning to its original position. </p><p>A Chicago Fire Department boat could be seen spraying water on the structure, apparently to cool it down. Chicago was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/01/september-october-chicago-heat-wave-is-this-normal" target="_blank" >under a heat advisory</a> Wednesday. The temperature had reached 90 degrees by early afternoon.</p>

entries.title: Another Chicago bridge gets stuck in sweltering heat hours after DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge reopens
entries.summary: <p>Commuters faced headaches in multiple directions Wednesday as the Torrence Avenue Bridge got stuck in the raised position late Wednesday afternoon, just hours after the DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge reopened following a similar occurrence.</p><p>The city’s Office of Emergency Management and Communications <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/ChicagoOEMC/status/2095290854676038104?s=20" target="_blank" ><u>confirmed</u></a> via social media at 6:20 p.m. that the Torrence Avenue Bridge — located over the Calumet River on Far South Side — was “stuck in the up position” and said hot weather caused the issue. The office urged drivers to use alternate routes.</p><p>The bridge — located over the Calumet River — was stuck for more than an hour, starting at 4:30 p.m., according to Erica Schroeder, director of public affairs for the Chicago Department of Transportation.</p><p>Schroeder confirmed the issue with the Torrence Avenue bridge was heat-related.</p><p>"Thermal expansion caused by the high temperatures affected the bridge’s operation," Schroeder explained.</p><p>CDOT crews responded to the scene and returned the bridge to its normal operating position, Schroeder said. The bridge was reopened to traffic by 5:30 p.m.</p><p>Just hours earlier, the DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge was reopened to traffic Wednesday afternoon, over four hours after the bridge became stuck open during a routine lift.</p><p>With the bridge unable to close all the way, traffic was snarled up and down the drive.</p><p>The bridge over the Chicago River "experienced a heat-related issue preventing it from fully closing" around 10 a.m. after it was lifted for a large yacht to pass beneath, according to the Chicago Department of Transportation.</p><p>Crews then spent the next several hours trying to get the bridge to close completely. entries.title: In return from injured list, Davis Martin looked like the starting pitcher the White Sox need
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON – The biggest potential advantage for the Cleveland Guardians as they chase the White Sox in the American League Central standings is starting pitching.</p><p>With their pitching development engine, the Guardians once more have a deep rotation led by All-Star rookie Parker Messick. The White Sox’ top <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/18/white-sox-noah-schultz-hagen-smith-tanner-mcdougal-david-sandlin-brian-bannister-will-venable-erick-fedde-jose-urquidy-davis-martin-al-central" target="_blank" ><u>pitching prospects have been getting a lesson in how development isn’t linear</u></a>, and the club has spent the summer piecing their rotation together with bullpen games and openers.</p><p>Opening day starter Shane Smith is working in relief now. Of their four-best pitching prospects, only Hagen Smith is in the majors and is also in the bullpen. The biggest potential source of stability for the Sox rotation down the stretch was just activated off the injured list in Davis Martin, who issued a reminder of such with 5 2/3 scoreless innings Wednesday night against the Astros.</p><p>The best argument in favor of Martin’s ability to suddenly become a rotation anchor in the final month is that he’s done it before–this season. Even the yeoman back-end starter version of Martin from years past would be a boost for the Sox. But as he carried a 2.00 ERA and 27% strikeout rate through Memorial Day this year, Martin looked bound for an All-Star appearance and like someone who could start a playoff game.</p><p>“He was really suppressing damage,” said Sox senior advisor to pitching Brian Bannister. “I think it's his ability to diversify his pitches to hit different parts of the zone with different shapes.”</p><p>At his best, the 29-year-old right-hander’s command of a six-pitch mix lends him an improvisational style. In an age of hyper-intentional gameplanning, Martin is the rare starter who is really out there reading swings and pitching with guile to lift his results above his pure stuff.</p><p>Even as his performance wavered, and he entered Wednesday night with a 7.06 ERA since June 1, the White Sox have expressed confidence they have the video and biomechanical information to return Martin to his baselines.</p><p>“With him and with all the guys, we know what good looks like,” said pitching coach Zach Bove.</p><p>Almost every pitcher has some weaknesses baked into their strengths, and Martin is no different. The arm action that gives him great feel for spinning breaking balls and even enables his wonky kick-changeup, also asks a lot from his body over the long haul.</p><p>“He kind of drops his arm down and it's a very arm-heavy delivery, so there's definitely an element of fatigue,” Bannister told the Sun-Times. “You see that in just the velocities.”</p><p>Per FanGraphs, Martin averaged 94.2 mph on his four-seam fastball through May, and 93.6 mph since. That’s a real dip, but also small enough for Martin and the Sox to focus more on command. When he slouches in his posture on the mound, his arm will dip alongside it and suddenly his six-pitch mix shrinks to trying to groove fastballs to get back in the count. When he began overcorrecting to the point of leaning backwards, it was no good either.</p><p>“Just one little change, and then it just keeps snowballing,” Martin said. “You just think everything's going fine, and then all of a sudden you're just out of luck. Over the course of 162 games, that happens.”</p><p>Fittingly, the Sox seized upon Martin developing a middle finger blister just as his results reached their nadir as an opportunity for both a rest and reset. He only had a single five-inning Triple-A rehab outing, but the club saw proof of concept.</p><p>“The delivery stuff that he had been working on when he was on IL, it showed out,” said Bove.</p><p>In striking out three and walking just one on Wednesday, touching 96 mph, and cutting through the heart of the Houston batting order to wriggle out of a third-inning jam that saw runners at the corners with no one out, Martin furthered his case that he can be the starter the Sox need.</p>

entries.title: Chicago extends program offering free Wifi to CPS students
entries.summary: <p>More than 28,000 Chicago Public Schools students will have access to free internet at home this year thanks to the extension of the Chicago Connected program.</p><p>The program launched in 2020 in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and a shift to remote learning. Since then, more than 60,000 students have gained access to reliable home internet to complete homework and access online resources, the city of Chicago said in a news release.</p><p>“Making sure that our young people and families have access to Wifi, the internet, it's a critical component of their development,” Mayor Brandon Johnson told the Sun-Times. “As a former public school teacher, I know how important it is for students to have access to the world, to the internet.”</p><p>About $2 million was dedicated to the effort, with much of the up-front costs covered by the continuation of service from prior years, according to a city spokesman. </p><p>The Department of Technology and Innovation saved money by moving IT services to the cloud and other cost-saving measures, meaning the cost of the program could be funded by CPS and the city instead of through partnerships with internet providers and community organizations.</p><p>Around 93% of the program’s families were categorized as economically disadvantaged, and almost all of the 20 community areas with the largest improvement in connectivity rates are on the South and West Sides of the city.</p><p>“That economic disadvantage did not go away with the pandemic; the pandemic exposed what many of us have always known, that the world is cut off from families who are historically left out,” Johnson said.</p><p>Families also noted internet access benefitted them beyond schooling, helping with email communication and searching for information online, according to the news release. Johnson said he’s heard from families who are also able to stay in contact with family members when they’re away from the home, like a student whose marching band practices can go late into the evening.</p><p>“It becomes, really, a safety mechanism, where they're able to monitor the whereabouts of their loved ones,” Johnson said. “It's those kinds of elements that I think people sometimes take for granted.”</p>

entries.title: Cubs need to lose bullpen blues to be best version of themselves come October: ‘These are guys we count on’
entries.summary: <p>In a 162-game season, bullpen pitchers are going to have bad stretches.</p><p>Sometimes, those stretches are going to overlap.</p><p>There’s nothing terribly abnormal about what the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> are experiencing right now, a string of bad days for the relief corps.</p><p>But it’s the time of year when the lights are getting bright. A bullpen that has been generally effective throughout much of the summer is having a rough go at a bad time.</p><p>In the span of 11 games, righty closer <b>Jacob Webb</b> coughed up walk-off home runs in consecutive outings, righty <b>Trent Thornton</b> was rocked for six runs and three homers in a pair of appearances against the Reds, and righty fireballer <b>Daniel Palencia</b> gave up the lead to the Brewers, balking a run home and serving up a game-flipping homer — though he was one of four relievers to combine to allow six runs in that loss.</p><p>Not great.</p><p>Though there are several notable pitchers either rehabbing from injury or stashed in the minor leagues — righties <b>Edward Cabrera</b>, <b>Shelby Miller</b> and <b>Javier Assad</b>, plus lefty <b>Justin Steele</b> — it’s unknown how likely it is that those guys, aside from Assad, make significant contributions to the relief unit.</p><p>Instead of waiting for saviors, the Cubs are focused on steadying this group before the season’s most important games.</p><p>“You try to figure out: How are we going to be our best team? And it’s with these guys pitching well,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Wednesday. “These are the guys we need to pitch well. The way to do that is to get them back out there and have them pitch again.</p><p>“You get beat. And it’s no fun, and it stinks. But if you’re not confident, that’s how you get your confidence back. If you’re struggling with something, that’s how you find it. You find it out there on the field, when the competition’s going on and the other side’s trying to get you.</p><p>“These are guys we count on, and we need them. And the best way for us to be the best team is to get them back out there.”</p><p>These games, though, are important, too.</p><p>These bullpen blues could be a passing bummer. But any lingering problems could prove exceptionally costly down the stretch and into the playoffs.</p><h3><b>Justin time?</b></h3><p>Steele made his long-awaited return to game action Wednesday, making a minor league rehab appearance with Triple-A Iowa.</p><p>Steele has been out since April of last season, recovering from elbow surgery and a setback earlier this year.</p><p>He faced 10 batters Wednesday, retiring five of them and allowing three runs, only one earned, on four hits.</p><p>Though Steele is hopeful this is the next step in a return to the major league mound this season, Cubs brass has cautioned against assuming the southpaw will be able to pitch out of the team’s bullpen before the campaign’s end.</p><p>“I’m excited for him that he’s getting back out there,” team president <b>Jed Hoyer</b> said Tuesday. “As it relates to this team, we’ll see. We’re not in development mode at this point.</p><p>“If he can come back and he can help us, he’s going to come back and he’s going to help us. If there’s rust and he needs more time, it’s not the time to do that.</p><p>“I’m very open-minded, but I don’t know how this is going to go.”</p><h3><b>Ramirez sits again</b></h3><p>The Cubs kept infielder <b>Pedro Ramirez</b> out of the lineup for a third consecutive game Wednesday as he recovers from back spasms that popped up Sunday.</p><p>“I expect him to make a full recovery and be good entries.title: Playing time could be sparse for White Sox' right-handed outfielders down the stretch
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON — <b>Randal Grichuk</b>’s two-run double off Astros reliever <b>Tatsuya Imai</b> broke open the White Sox’ 5-1 victory on Tuesday. But the bigger development was Grichuk getting an opportunity to face right-handed pitching at all.</p><p>The 35-year-old’s brilliance as a midseason pickup has been his ability to mash left-handed pitching on command. While his spot in the lineup against right-handed starter <b>Ronel Blanco</b> was partially about a rest day for rookie <b>Braden Montgomery</b>, it also was about not letting Grichuk rust during a long absence of traditional opportunities.</p><p>“Minnesota, back home, it’s going to be all righties,” Grichuk said of the coming series against the Twins. “Sprinkle some at-bats in, to where it’s not a huge layoff, definitely huge for feel and the rhythm.”</p><p>Manager <b>Will Venable</b> loves playing platoon matchups, and hunting value on the margins remains vital as the Sox push to clinch the American League Central title. Simultaneously, the presence of newly acquired right-handed outfielders <b>Brenton Doyle</b> and <b>Tommy Pham</b>,<b> </b>alongside Grichuk, give the Sox a host of players they want to keep active in some form.</p><p>“We’re going to have to figure out how to keep them involved,” Venable said. “There will be [pinch-hit] opportunities during the game. I’m not sure exactly how we’ll get them starts, to be honest.”</p><p>To drive the point home, Venable admitted utilityman Luisangel Acuña likely won’t start a game all this week.</p><p>“We’ve been transparent with them about what it looks like for them over this next stretch,” Venable said.</p><h3><b>From opening day starter to Triple-A reliever</b></h3><p><b>Shane Smith</b>’s last two outings with Triple-A Charlotte have been in relief, as the White Sox abandon ideas of restoring his place in the rotation this year. Those outings have also both been scoreless.</p><p>“He's an option,” Venable said of Smith’s chances of contributing to the major league bullpen. “I was looking at videos today, I think he looks really good.”</p><h3><b>Vasil has a date</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Dugout cheerleader extraordinaire <b>Mike Vasil </b>rushed from the airport to the ballpark Tuesday night to celebrate a victory with teammates, but he also had personal reasons to smile. Vasil’s visit to Dr. Keith Meister in Dallas saw him cleared to play catch on Sept. 18, which will be his first time throwing since undergoing Tommy John surgery.</p><p>“As much fun as I’ve had, it’s not even close to the same as actually playing,” Vasil said.</p><h3><b>Brazoban begins rehab</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Eight days after being placed on the injured list with a strained left lat muscle, right-handed reliever <b>Huascar Brazoban</b> began a Triple-A rehab assignment on Wednesday.</p><p>That normally would suggest a swift return for an important White Sox trade-deadline acquisition, but Brazoban allowed six runs in his last five innings before his injury, and the Sox want to see a return to form before he’s activated.</p><p>“The key with him is execute the changeup,” pitching coach Zach Bove told the Sun-Times. “So [hitters] have to honor something else. Because if not, then he’s boxed into being pretty much a one-pitch guy.”</p><h3><b>Bush and Berroa update</b></h3><h3></h3><p>After both underwent Tommy John surgery in spring 2025, <b>Ky Bush </b>and <b>Prelander Berroa</b> have also been sidelined all this year with setbacks in their rehab process.</p><p>Bush is officially done for the season due to a left lat strain, while Berroa will throw off a mound again next week for the first time since May.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true"
